traveler: Rollo (Hrolfr, Gongu-Hrolfr, Robert of Rouen), first ruler of the Northmen of the Seine
title: The Whale Road to the Epte: the Northman, the Ford, and the One Surviving Parchment
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Out of the North: the Two Traditions

stops.name: Central Scandinavia, a birth with no record
stops.date_confidence: Birth date and place unknown. English Wikipedia gives two competing traditions, c. 835 and c. 870, rather than a range; the tomb epitaph implies the 850s by calling him over eighty at a death in 933. No source names a birthplace, a year, or a parent that any other source confirms. The pin is a generic point in central Scandinavia and the year 860 is chosen only to open the sequence.
stops.campa: He is born in the north, and the north does not write. No annal of Denmark or of Norway records the year, the farm, or the father, and the first parchment that will ever carry his name is a Frankish charter he will not see for sixty years. Two peoples will claim him afterward and each will build him a lineage running backward from the sea. What the century agrees on is the direction of travel: south and west, down the whale road, in ships that come home heavier than they went out.
suggested_refs: The unresolved Danish and Norwegian origin traditions, set out in Robert Helmerichs, 'The Rollonid Principality: Rollo', ORB
sources: D. C. Douglas, 'Rollo of Normandy', English Historical Review 57 (1942)

stops.name: Jutland, the father's land in Dudo's Dacia
stops.date_confidence: Dudo of Saint-Quentin's account alone, written c. 996-1015, three generations after the events; no Danish source names the father, the brother Gurim, or the exile. Dudo's 'Dacia' is not straightforwardly Denmark: he reaches the identification through a false etymology joining Daci to Dani, Dacia properly denoting the lower Danube and Black Sea region. Coordinates mark central Jutland as a stand-in; Dudo names no site. The year orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: Dudo puts the family in Dacia, by which he means Denmark, and gives the boy a father who holds wide land there and a brother called Gurim. The father dies, a king falls on the house, and Gurim is killed in the field. What Dudo has built by that point is not a raider by appetite but a dispossessed heir, so that whatever is taken later is only taken back. Then he sends him out of the story's first country: to the ships, with whatever men will follow him, off a coast that has no room left for him.
stops.quote: No region brings forth extraordinary men, and ones actively instructed in arms, more than does Dacia.
stops.quote_source: King Alstem of the Angles, on the Dacians; Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Felice Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 7
suggested_refs: Dudo's Dacia and the Daci-Dani etymology, discussed in Wikipedia, 'Rollo'
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Felice Lifshitz, ORB online edition, chs. 7 and 12, http://the-orb.arlima.net/orb_done/dudo/07-vision

stops.name: Møre, the earl's son of the sagas
stops.date_confidence: Orkneyinga saga and Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla, both thirteenth century, some three hundred years after Rollo. The identification of Gongu-Hrolfr with Rollo of Rouen is a later Icelandic and Norwegian tradition and is attested in no Frankish source. The date is set only so this tradition sits beside the Danish one; the two cannot be combined into a single biography.
stops.campa: The other tradition is Norwegian and it comes in verse. Snorri Sturluson names him Hrolfr, son of Rognvaldr Eysteinsson, earl of Møre, and of Hildr the daughter of Hrolfr Nefja. Two nations are building the same ancestor here, and a Danish heir dispossessed by a king is not the same man as a Norwegian earl's son; the stories will not join. What the Norwegian one adds is a body. They call him Gangr, the Walker, because no horse in the country can carry him, so he goes to the raiding and comes home from it on his own feet.
suggested_refs: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, 'Harald Harfager's Saga', ch. 24, 'Rolf Ganger Driven into Banishment'
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Haralds saga harfagra ch. 24, trans. Samuel Laing, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/598/598-h/598-h.htm

stops.name: Giske, the island that keeps the claim
stops.date_confidence: Regional tradition, carried by the Fjord Norway tourism authority. Correction to the research pool: the cited 'Wikipedia, Giske' is a disambiguation page, and the Giske Municipality article does not mention Rognvald Eysteinsson, the Møre earls, or Gange-Rolv at all. Coordinates are the municipality's own stated point; the pool's 62.4794, 6.0339 falls offshore. Nothing in the sagas places Hrolfr himself here. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Off Ålesund the low island of Giske holds the seat that Norway attaches to the earls of Møre, and so to the father the sagas give him. Nothing in the sagas puts Hrolfr himself on this ground; what lives here is the claim. The fjord country keeps the name Gange-Rolv the way the Seine keeps Rollo, as a local man who went out and came back a country. Farms on the island have been worked without a break since before his century, and the sound between it and the mainland runs straight out to open water.
suggested_refs: Fjord Norway, 'The Town Park in Ålesund', on the Giske and Gange-Rolv tradition
sources: Fjord Norway tourism authority, 'The Town Park in Ålesund'
Wikipedia, 'Giske (municipality)', checked and negative for Rollo material

stops.name: Viken, cattle taken against the king's ban
stops.date_confidence: Heimskringla, Harald Harfager's Saga ch. 24, written c. 1225. A saga-only episode with no contemporary corroboration, belonging to the Norwegian tradition, which the Danish tradition in Dudo contradicts outright. Date set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Harald Fairhair has forbidden all plundering inside Norway, and whoever raids at home raids the king himself. Coming in off a summer of sea-work, Hrolfr puts men ashore in Viken, on the fjord that will one day be Oslo's, and takes cattle for the ship's meat. It is a small theft and the law behind it is not small. The herd is a farmer's, the farmer is the king's, and the ban is how Harald holds a country he took piece by piece. Word goes up the coast before the beasts are butchered.
suggested_refs: Harald Fairhair's ban on plundering within Norway, Heimskringla ch. 24
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Haralds saga harfagra ch. 24, trans. Samuel Laing

stops.name: Avaldsnes, the Thing that makes him an outlaw
stops.date_confidence: Heimskringla ch. 24 names no place for the assembly; it says only that the king assembled a Thing. Correction to the research pool: its 'Harald Fairhair's court' pin at 59.9, 6.05 falls on uninhabited highland between Hardanger and Røldal. The stop is moved to Avaldsnes on Karmøy, Harald's attested royal seat, so it sits on real ground. Thirteenth-century saga tradition throughout; month arbitrary.
stops.campa: The king calls a Thing and has Hrolfr declared an outlaw, and the sentence carries the whole country with it: no roof anywhere in Norway and no court to appeal to. Harald has spent his life forcing one law to hold from Agder to Halogaland, and he will not spend that on an earl's son who took cattle at home. Hildr his mother comes and asks for the judgement back, and asks in verse, because a plea to a king is a made thing and must be made well. She calls the anger a thing that drives wolves out of the land. The king does not give way.
stops.quote: Think'st thou, King Harald, in thy anger, To drive away my brave Rolf Ganger Like a mad wolf, from out the land?
stops.quote_source: Hild, mother of Rolf Ganger, to King Harald Fairhair; Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Harald Harfager's Saga ch. 24, trans. Samuel Laing
suggested_refs: Avaldsnes on Karmøy, Harald Fairhair's royal seat
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Haralds saga harfagra ch. 24, trans. Samuel Laing

stops.name: The Hebrides, west through the Sudreys
stops.date_confidence: Correction to the research pool: this waypoint is Heimskringla ch. 24, not the Orkneyinga saga; the Gutenberg Orkneyinga text cited there contains no Gange-Rolv banishment passage. The saga names no island and no landing, so the pin is Lewis, standing for the Sudreyjar generally. Thirteenth-century tradition; date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Out of Norway he goes the way outlawed men go, west over the sea to the Sudreys, the southern isles the Norse hold off Scotland. There are crews there already sailing under their own names and no king's peace, and the islands are full of men who left Norway under the same sentence he is carrying. Among them an exile with a following can find ships. Which island, which winter, whose hall: Snorri names none of it, and gives the whole remainder of the life in one sentence.
stops.quote: Rolf Ganger went afterwards over sea to the West to the Hebrides, or Sudreys; and at last farther west to Valland, where he plundered and subdued for himself a great earldom, which he peopled with Northmen, from which that land is called Normandy.
stops.quote_source: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Harald Harfager's Saga ch. 24, trans. Samuel Laing
suggested_refs: The Norse Sudreyjar, the southern isles, as a staging ground for westward exile
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Haralds saga harfagra ch. 24, trans. Samuel Laing, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/598/598-h/598-h.htm

stops.name: East Anglia, King Alstem and the mountain of birds
stops.date_confidence: Dudo ch. 7 only. 'Alstem' is sometimes equated with Guthrum or with Aethelstan of East Anglia; neither identification is secure and no English source connects Rollo to either. Correction to the research pool: Alstem does not interpret the dream. The mountain-and-birds vision is expounded by an unnamed Christian captive taken in battle. Helmerichs notes Dudo habitually transfers other Viking leaders' adventures onto Rollo. Coordinates are Norwich, a generic East Anglian point; date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Among the Angles he takes a Christian prisoner in battle, and the prisoner reads him a dream: a mountain, a spring at its foot, birds of many kinds bathing in the water and building their nests together up the slope. The mountain is Francia, the captive tells him, the spring is baptism, and the birds are peoples who will come to him out of everywhere and hold one land under one law. Rollo frees the man, loads him with gifts, and sends him home. Then he sends envoys to King Alstem and makes a peace.
stops.quote: Our lord and advocate Rollo, mightiest patrician of all and most distinguished duke of the Dacians, sends faithful service to you and the gift of unshattered friendship to your followers.
stops.quote_source: Rollo's ambassadors to King Alstem of the Angles; Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Felice Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 7
suggested_refs: Dudo's vision of the mountain and the birds, History of the Normans ch. 7, the legitimating dream of the Norman foundation
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 7, http://the-orb.arlima.net/orb_done/dudo/07-vision

stops.name: Walcheren, the Frisians and the storm
stops.date_confidence: Dudo only, and unverifiable. Helmerichs (ORB) notes that Dudo routinely attaches other Viking leaders' exploits to Rollo, and no contemporary source places Rollo at Walcheren. Coordinates approximate the island; Dudo names no landing point. Date arbitrary, set to order the crossing.
stops.campa: The crossing from England to the Frankish shore goes wrong. Weather scatters the fleet down among the mouths of the Scheldt, and the Frisians of Walcheren come out to meet whatever the storm has left, boat against boat in the shallows off the island. The Frisians know these channels and he does not, which is most of what a fight in shallow water amounts to. He wins there anyway, and does not stay. Ahead of him is the mouth of the Seine, and up the Seine is everything the century has taught him is worth the taking.
suggested_refs: Dudo's pre-911 itinerary, discussed critically in ORB, 'The Rollonid Principality: Rollo'
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition

stops.name: Paris, the siege of the island
stops.date_confidence: The siege itself is fully historical, 25 November 885 to October 886, fought at the two fortified bridgeheads of the Île de la Cité. Rollo's personal participation is NOT secured by any contemporary source naming him: ORB states this flatly, and the tradition placing him there is later. Coordinates are the atlas's canonical Paris pin rather than the island's own centre.
stops.campa: In November the Northmen come up the Seine and stop at the two bridges that tie the island to its banks, seven hundred ships and a winter to spend. They build engines, fire the towers, mine the bridgeheads, and the city holds. In April the leader Sigfred takes a payment and goes; part of the fleet stays on in the country round about, and the tradition written a century later keeps Rollo among those who stay. In October the emperor comes down with an army and pays them to winter in Burgundy instead.
suggested_refs: The fortified bridgeheads of the Île de la Cité, held through the winter of 885-886

stops.name: Bayeux, the taking of Poppa
stops.date_confidence: Dudo only; he dates the capture to 885 or 889 and no contemporary source records it. His wording describes conquest and captivity and establishes no consent; 'marriage more danico' is a modern historians' label, not his term. Poppa's parentage is contested: Christian Settipani makes her a daughter of Guy de Senlis, Katherine Keats-Rohan a daughter of Berengar II of Neustria. The Planctus detail is attested (van Houts, Anglo-Norman Studies 36). Month arbitrary.
stops.campa: Bayeux is taken and put to the fire, and out of the wreck he takes Poppa, daughter of the count Berengar, and joins her to himself. Dudo writes the sentence as conquest and does not soften it: the town falls, the woman is seized, the woman bears him William. Later Normandy will call this a marriage in the Danish manner and set a statue of her up in the square. A lament sung after that son's murder says he was born overseas of a pagan father and a Christian mother.
suggested_refs: The modern statue of Poppa at the Place Charles de Gaulle, Bayeux (approx. 49.2782, -0.7047)
Elisabeth van Houts, 'The Planctus on the Death of William Longsword (943)', Anglo-Norman Studies 36 (2014)
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition
Elisabeth van Houts, Anglo-Norman Studies 36 (2014), Cambridge Core

stops.name: Rouen, the city taken and kept
stops.date_confidence: The date of Rollo's seizure of Rouen is disputed and no source fixes it; the English Wikipedia article flags it explicitly as unsettled. Rouen as his seat is secure, inferred from the language of the 918 diploma and from Flodoard, who from 925 calls his people the Northmen of Rouen. The year 900 is a placeholder set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Every other Frankish town he burns and leaves. Rouen he keeps. The archbishop's city on the tidal reach of the Seine has walls a fleet can shelter behind, a bridge, a mint, and a river that carries seagoing ships up to its quays and river craft down from Paris. He does not sack it. He moves into it. From here the Northmen of the Seine become a thing with an address, which is what a king can negotiate with, and the Roumois and the Pays de Caux feed the place through the winters.
suggested_refs: The Roumois and the Pays de Caux, the earliest secure territory of the Rouen principality
sources: Flodoard of Reims, Annals, entries from 925

segments.name: Chartres and the Bargain at the Ford

stops.name: Chartres, the defeat beneath the walls
stops.date_confidence: Battle and date attested: FranceArchives gives 20 juillet 911 and names the Frankish coalition as Robert, marquis of Neustria, Ebles Manzer, count of Poitiers, and Richard, duke of Burgundy. Corrections to the research pool: Bishop Gantelmus is not named in that source and Ebles Manzer was omitted from it. Contradiction left standing: FranceArchives says Rollo led the defeated Scandinavians and suffered 'une grave défaite', while ORB states flatly that no contemporary evidence ties Rollo to Chartres and that Dudo credits him with it by his usual pattern of attribution.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of July a Frankish coalition comes up on the besiegers under the walls of Chartres: Robert, marquis of Neustria, Ebles Manzer, count of Poitiers, and Richard, duke of Burgundy. The Northmen are broken there and driven off the field. A king who has just won can afford to give away a province, which is why what follows is a settlement and not another payment. It is the first time in a generation that the Franks have caught a Seine fleet on land and beaten it.
suggested_refs: The walls of Chartres, under which the Scandinavian force was broken on 20 July 911

stops.name: Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, from the Epte to the sea
stops.date_confidence: No treaty text survives and no contemporary document names Saint-Clair-sur-Epte; the place, the date, the boundaries, and the clauses are all reconstructed from Dudo a century later. FranceArchives places a negotiated settlement in the second half of 911, after Chartres. The Gisla marriage carries a standing chronological objection: Charles III first married in May 907, so a legitimate daughter could be at most about four years old in 911, which leads historians to treat her as illegitimate, as a child betrothal, or as Dudo's invention. October is conventional.
stops.campa: Charles the Simple sends to the camp and the terms come back: the land from the river Epte down to the sea, in Rollo's hand and his heirs' after him, in exchange for baptism, for service, and for the defence of the kingdom against whatever else comes up the Seine. The king adds his daughter Gisla to it. Two provinces' worth of Francia changes hands at a ford on a small river, on the word of the men standing at it. No parchment is drawn. Who stood there, and what was actually promised, is a thing nobody afterward can say.
suggested_refs: GRHis, Université de Rouen, '911-2011: le traité de Saint-Clair-sur-Epte et l'identité normande'
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 12

stops.name: Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, the foot that is not kissed
stops.date_confidence: The scene is Dudo's alone, written c. 996-1015, with no contemporary corroboration; Alice Taylor argues he exaggerated an ordinary gesture of homage rather than recording an event. Both spoken lines are verified verbatim against the Lifshitz translation. Correction to the research pool: that translation is not on Fordham, whose Dudo path returns HTTP 500 with no Wayback capture. It is the ORB edition, ch. 12, equal to Lair Bk. II ch. 29.
stops.campa: The grant is made and the bishops name the form it has to take. He is to kneel and kiss the king's foot. He will not. The bishops press him, because the gesture is the transaction itself: a man who does not kneel has not become anybody's man, and the land stays granted only if he does. In the end a man of his is deputed to do it in his place, and rather than go down he takes hold of the king's foot and lifts it to his own mouth where he stands. Charles goes over backward in front of his own court. The Franks laugh.
stops.quote: I will never kneel before the knees of another, nor will I kiss anyone's foot.
stops.quote_source: Rollo to the Frankish bishops; Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Felice Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 12
suggested_refs: Dudo, History of the Normans ch. 12, the foot-kiss episode; Alice Taylor's reading of it as an exaggerated gesture of homage
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 12, http://the-orb.arlima.net/orb_done/dudo/12-franco

stops.name: Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, the hands in the king's hands
stops.date_confidence: Dudo only, and the day is an ordering device, not a record. Flodoard, the near-contemporary source, calls Rollo princeps, a flexible word for leader; 'first Duke of Normandy' is a retrospective title, not an office attested in his lifetime. The quoted line is verified verbatim in the Lifshitz translation, ORB ch. 12, exclamation points and all.
stops.campa: What he does agree to do he does in front of everyone. He puts his hands inside the king's hands, which is the Frankish gesture and means what it means: a man with a fleet becomes a man with a lord. The Franks standing round have been fighting him for twenty-five years and say so out loud while he is doing it, admiringly, as men do about an enemy who has just become theirs. Dudo calls him duke in that sentence, half a century before any Norman ruler is called one.
stops.quote: That is the duke, so powerful! so valorous! so resolute and discreet! so hard-working! who has prosecuted such great battles against the counts of this realm.
stops.quote_source: The Franks at Saint-Clair-sur-Epte; Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 12
suggested_refs: Flodoard's princeps against Dudo's dux: the vocabulary of Rollo's authority
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 12
Flodoard of Reims, Annals, entries for 925 and 928

stops.name: Rouen, the font and the name Robert
stops.date_confidence: Dudo gives 'the nine hundred and twelfth year from the incarnation' and names Archbishop Franco as baptizer and Robert of Neustria, the future King Robert I, as godfather. No contemporary witness confirms the date, the officiant, or the sponsor. The seven days of army baptism and the distribution of gifts to churches are likewise Dudo's alone. Month and day default to January.
stops.campa: Archbishop Franco baptizes him in the cathedral church of Rouen, and Robert, duke of the Franks, lifts him out of the water and gives him his own name. The Northman is Robert now, in the font and afterward in the charters, though nobody will call him that for a thousand years. His captains and his army follow him in over seven days, beginning at Rouen and going on to Bayeux, and he goes round the churches of his new country giving back a share of what his fleet took out of them.
stops.quote: archbishop Franco has baptized Rollo, imbued with the catholic faith of the sacrosanct Trinity, and Robert, duke of the Franks, has taken him up from the font of the Savior and given his own name to him
stops.quote_source: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 13
suggested_refs: Rouen Cathedral, church of the baptism and, twenty years later, of the burial
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 13, http://the-orb.arlima.net/orb_done/dudo/13-reign

stops.name: Bayeux, the church raised out of the burning
stops.date_confidence: The rebuilding is Norman ecclesiastical memory attributed to Rollo personally; no charter and no archaeological evidence supports the attribution. Two of the three Carolingian churches at Bayeux had been destroyed in the raids, and the site of the largest is where the later cathedral stands. The 1046 fire and the present Gothic church are attested. Date arbitrary, placed after the baptism.
stops.campa: Of the three Carolingian churches at Bayeux the raids have left one standing. He puts a building back on the site of the largest of the ruined ones, quickly and out of little, and the new Christian of Rouen becomes a founder in a town he had burned to the ground a quarter of a century before. Two great churches will stand on this ground after his: a Romanesque cathedral that goes up and burns in 1046, and the Gothic one that replaces it, which is where the Tapestry will be kept.
suggested_refs: Bayeux Cathedral, successor on the site of the church attributed to Rollo's rebuilding

stops.name: The Seine valley, the converts who go back
stops.date_confidence: Datable to 914: Hervé was archbishop of Reims 900-922 and John X pope from March 914, and the consultation belongs to that year. This corrects the research pool, which dated it vaguely 'before 928' and so lost the point, which is that the relapse is documented two years after the traditional baptism. Attested through ORB's summary of the ecclesiastical notices. The evidence concerns the Seine Northmen as a community; Rollo is not named personally in it. The pin is the Seine valley, where the converts were, not Reims, where the letter was written.
stops.campa: Two years after the font, Archbishop Hervé of Reims writes to Pope John X about the baptized Northmen of the Seine. They have gone back. They are killing Christians and killing priests, sacrificing to idols and eating the meat of the sacrifices, and the archbishop wants to know how hard the church may come down on them. A people is not converted in a day at a font, and Hervé has the whole province to keep. The pope answers that severity would only drive them further into their old errors, and counsels patience.
suggested_refs: The correspondence of Archbishop Hervé of Reims with Pope John X, 914, on the relapsed Northmen of the Seine

stops.name: Longpaon, the ploughshare and the fire
stops.date_confidence: Dudo's exemplum, ch. 13: a literary illustration of imposed peace, not a preserved law and not a court record. Lifshitz's own note identifies Longpaon as modern Darnétal, which is where the pin sits. The date is arbitrary. The ordeal ends with the wife beaten into confession and both husband and wife hanged as thieves, which Dudo reports approvingly.
stops.campa: He has banned theft in his country and banned it absolutely: a farmer is to leave his tools in the furrow overnight and find them there in the morning. At Longpaon a ploughman's irons go missing anyway. The wife is the one who took them and hid them, and she is also the one who sends her husband to court to complain about the loss. Robert hears him out, pays him five solidi to replace what is gone, and sends an officer to the villa to find the thief by fire.
stops.quote: Give this farmer five solidi with which to replace what he has lost. You make for the villa as quickly as possible and, through trial by fire, search out the author of the theft.
stops.quote_source: Rollo, under his baptismal name Robert, to a manorial agent; Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 13
suggested_refs: Longpaon, today Darnétal, near Rouen, site of Dudo's ordeal by fire
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 13

stops.name: The forest of Roumare, the ring left hanging
stops.date_confidence: The ring-on-the-branch motif is later Norman folklore and resembles the Scandinavian Peace of Frodi; Dudo's documented core is the ploughshare ordeal, not the ring. Gilduin Davy (English Historical Review) shows that the 'laws of Rollo' assembled from such material were substantially an early-modern construction by historians and lawyers. Coordinates approximate the forest on the Seine's northern loop; no source fixes a site. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: The peace becomes a story the country tells about itself. In the forest of Roumare, across the great loop of the Seine from Rouen, a gold ring hangs on a branch for years and nobody takes it down. It is the oldest boast a hard ruler gets, older than Normandy: the Danes told it of Frodi's peace before there were Normans to tell it of anyone. The woman who lost her husband to the ploughshare ordeal is in the same chapter, and she gets the last word in it.
stops.quote: Useless man, now go to duke Robert and let him turn you into a ploughman himself.
stops.quote_source: The farmer's wife, of duke Robert, spoken with scolding and sarcasm; Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 13
suggested_refs: Gilduin Davy, 'The Laws of Rollo', English Historical Review 138 (2023)
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 13
Gilduin Davy, 'The Laws of Rollo', English Historical Review, https://academic.oup.com/ehr/article/138/594-595/1255/7504767

stops.name: Rouen, the land apportioned and the law laid on
stops.date_confidence: Dudo's summary statement, ch. 13, sitting in a list of achievements and quoting no law text anywhere in his work; the only concrete legislation he reports is the ban on theft and the prohibition on carrying plough tools home. Gilduin Davy has shown the 'laws of Rollo' known to later jurists were substantially constructed and rewritten in the early modern period. No tenth-century text of any such law survives. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: He divides the land among the men who came over with him, measures it out by rope, and sets them to rebuild what the fleet spent thirty years knocking down: walls, churches, mills, the defences along the river. Then he puts law on the people, ratified by the will of the leaders, and compels them to keep peace with one another. Dudo says so in one line and quotes not a single clause of it. Nothing that could be called a code of Rollo survives from the tenth century in any form at all.
stops.quote: he enjoined upon the populace rights and eternal laws, ratified and ordained by the will of the leaders
stops.quote_source: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 13
suggested_refs: The early-modern manufacture of a Rollonian founding constitution, per Gilduin Davy
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 13
Gilduin Davy, 'The Laws of Rollo', English Historical Review

stops.name: Compiègne, the diploma of the second ides of March
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and the strongest single item in this file: the original parchment survives as Archives nationales K 16, no. 9, and the Latin is verified verbatim against the CARO transcription. The diploma proves Rollo existed, led a group recognized and identified with the Seine by 918, and had already received a royal land grant for a defensive function. It dates no earlier grant, and so proves nothing about 911, Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, the boundaries, the marriage, or any ducal title. Corrections to the research pool: CARO is 'Chartes originales antérieures à 1121 conservées en France', not the Chartae Latinae Antiquiores corpus, and the abbey granted is La Croix-Saint-Ouen, given to Saint-Germain-des-Prés, not the other way round.
stops.campa: In the royal palace at Compiègne, Charles the Simple gives the abbey of La Croix-Saint-Ouen, on the Eure in the pagus of Madrie, to Saint-Germain-des-Prés and its monks for their table. One clause excepts the part of it he has already conceded to the Northmen of the Seine, namely Rollo and his companions, for the protection of the kingdom. The parchment is written, sealed, dated the second ides of March, and kept. Here is the man in the record: in a subordinate clause, inside an exemption, in somebody else's grant.
stops.quote: praeter partem ipsius abbatiȩ quam annuimus Normannis Sequanensibus, videlicet Rolloni suisque comitibus, pro tutela regni
stops.quote_source: Diploma of Charles III, Compiègne, 14 March 918; surviving original, Archives nationales K 16 no. 9, transcribed at CARO, caro.huma-num.fr
suggested_refs: Philippe Lauer, Recueil des actes de Charles III le Simple, vol. 1 (Paris, 1940)
sources: Original diploma, Archives nationales K 16 no. 9, transcription at https://caro.huma-num.fr/corpus/France/Charles_3/XCIIa

stops.name: Rouen, the ambassador from Robert of the Franks
stops.date_confidence: Dudo ch. 13 only, and both quoted lines are verified verbatim there. Correction to the research pool, which called the sender an unnamed rival duke: the ambassador comes from Robert, duke of the Franks, Rollo's own baptismal godfather and the future Robert I. Dudo places the episode after Gisla's death and immediately before the transfer of power to William, but the historical Robert opposed Charles in 922 and was killed at Soissons in June 923; Dudo's chronology here is elastic and fixes nothing. The date is chosen to sit between the 918 diploma and the 924 concessions.
stops.campa: Robert, duke of the Franks, the man who lifted him out of the font and gave him his own name, sends word to Rouen that he means to take the crown off Charles and drive him out of Francia, and wants the Northmen behind him. Gisla the king's daughter is dead by now, and whatever the marriage held together is finished with her. What comes back is neither a refusal nor an alliance. Burn the king's holdings, Rollo answers; I do not want him to have the rule.
stops.quote: With your advice and aid, I wish to take the kingship from Charles and chase him from Francia.
stops.quote_source: Robert, duke of the Franks, by ambassador to Robert of Rouen; Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 13
suggested_refs: Robert of Neustria, godfather at the font in 912 and king against Charles in 922
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 13

stops.name: The Bessin, the concession of 924
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Flodoard of Reims, Annals s.a. 924: with King Raoul's consent, further land, Maine and the Bessin, was conceded to the Northmen in a sworn peace. Whether the grant placed the Bessin under Rollo's personal control or under a wider Northmen coalition is disputed. Coordinates are Bayeux, standing for the region. Month not given.
stops.campa: Thirteen years on, under King Raoul and by another sworn peace, more land goes west: the Bessin, the country around Bayeux, added to what the Northmen already hold. It is less a gift than a ratification of where they have already got to. The duchy is not made at a ford in one afternoon; it is made in instalments, and each instalment is bought. Flodoard of Reims sets this one down in the year it happens, a canon writing at Reims with no reason at all to flatter anybody in Rouen.
suggested_refs: Flodoard of Reims, Annals, s.a. 924, on the sworn peace under King Raoul

stops.name: Maine, the grant that does not hold
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Flodoard s.a. 924 alongside the Bessin. Unlike the Bessin, Maine did not become a lasting part of Norman territory at this stage, and the grant may have conveyed tribute rights rather than settled possession. Coordinates are Le Mans, standing for the region; month arbitrary within the year.
stops.campa: The same sworn peace names Maine as well, the country running down toward Le Mans, and Maine does not stick. Le Mans is a bishop's city with counts of its own and no intention of taking a Northman for a lord. A grant made by a king who is fighting for his own throne is worth what the man receiving it can hold, and this one is not held. Whatever was conceded there, tribute rights or ground, the Northmen do not keep it, and the frontier of Normandy settles a long way north of Le Mans.
suggested_refs: The 924 concession of Maine, which left no lasting Norman frontier

stops.name: Beauvais, the district burned
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Flodoard, Annals s.a. 925, and the clearest contemporary evidence of organized violence under Rollo's leadership after his conversion. Coordinates mark the town, standing for the district; Flodoard names no landmark. Month not given.
stops.campa: In 925 the Northmen of Rouen break the peace they swore the year before and go out into the Beauvaisis, burning the countryside district by district. Fourteen years after the ford, thirteen after the army was baptized over seven days, eleven after the pope was asked what to do about the apostates, the Seine fleet is doing what the Seine fleet has always done. The Frankish answer comes back in kind, estates burned and cattle driven off in the Rouen country itself.
suggested_refs: Flodoard of Reims, Annals, s.a. 925, on the breaking of the peace by the Northmen of Rouen

stops.name: Amiens, the suburbs fired
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Flodoard s.a. 925. Coordinates mark the town, standing for the district; the tenth-century town predates the surviving Gothic cathedral by three centuries, so no extant landmark can be named. Month arbitrary within the campaign.
stops.campa: North and east from the Beauvaisis the same campaign takes in the district of Amiens and fires the town and its suburbs. There is no cathedral here yet worth the name: the Gothic church is three hundred years off, and what stands on the Somme is a walled Roman town with timber outside the walls. It is the timber that burns. Flodoard sets these entries down year by year at Reims as a canon keeping a record, and nothing in the annal explains why the peace broke.
suggested_refs: Flodoard of Reims, Annals, s.a. 925

stops.name: Noyon and Arras, the plunder carried on
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Flodoard s.a. 925 and 926. Corrections to the research pool: the French Wikipedia summary of Flodoard adds Arras to Beauvais, Amiens and Noyon, and ORB reports that the Franks besieged the Northmen's own stronghold of Eu and succeeded in capturing and destroying it, which the pool omitted. The 926 levy entry does not name Rollo. Coordinates are Noyon, standing for the wider raid; month arbitrary.
stops.campa: The raid runs on toward Noyon and takes in Arras, and by then it is a season's work rather than a raid. Then the Franks turn. King Raoul brings up an army, and instead of paying they go for the fortress the Northmen keep at Eu, take it, and pull it down. Burn, be beaten, be bought: the arrangement is thirty years old by now and nobody on either side proposes another. In 926 a levy is laid on Francia and Burgundy, collected in public, handed over, and the peace sworn again.
suggested_refs: Flodoard of Reims, Annals, s.a. 925 and 926, on the raid, the sack of Eu, and the renewed peace
sources: Flodoard of Reims, Annals, s.a. 925 and 926

stops.name: Eu, a thousand men sent up from Rouen
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Flodoard s.a. 925: when King Raoul mobilized, 'their princeps Rollo' sent 1,000 Northmen from Rouen to reinforce the fortress of Eu. Princeps is a flexible term for leader and is not evidence of a hereditary ducal title. Month arbitrary within the campaigning season. Only the castle chapel of the medieval fortress survives in the modern town.
stops.campa: When Raoul moves against the raiders, their princeps Rollo sends a thousand Northmen up from Rouen to hold the castle at Eu on the Bresle. Princeps is the only title a contemporary ever gives him and it means leader and nothing more precise than that. It is also the one place in the whole contemporary record where Rollo himself is shown giving an order. He is perhaps seventy years old. Of the fortress they held that summer, only the castle chapel is still standing in the town.
suggested_refs: The castle chapel at Eu, sole survivor of the fortress reinforced in 925

stops.name: Eu, the captive king produced
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Flodoard s.a. 927. Correction to the research pool, and it is material: Charles III was not a free participant. Herbert II of Vermandois had captured him in summer 923 at Château-Thierry and moved him to Péronne in 924, where he died in captivity on 7 October 929. Flodoard's entry records William's political act; Dudo later frames Rollo's withdrawal as a formal transfer of rule, which the annal does not say. Month not given.
stops.campa: Two years later the Franks come back to Eu, and the king they bring with them is not a free man. Charles the Simple has been Herbert of Vermandois's prisoner since 923, taken at Château-Thierry and held at Péronne, and Herbert brings him out to Eu to be commended to. William, Rollo's son, gives himself to Charles and in the same act swears friendship to Herbert, because the man holding the king is the fact in the room. Rollo is not named in the entry. The son is doing the business now.
suggested_refs: The captivity of Charles III at Péronne, 924 to his death on 7 October 929

stops.name: Rouen, the hostage Odo
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Flodoard s.a. 928, and the last securely dated appearance of Rollo as a living, politically active figure. Flodoard names no place; Rouen is used as his known seat, not a location the annal gives. Month not given. This entry rules out any death date earlier than 928.
stops.campa: The following year Rollo is holding Herbert of Vermandois's son Odo as a hostage, and will not give him back until Herbert, with bishops and counts behind him, has committed himself to King Charles, who is still in Herbert's own prison at Péronne. An old Northman on the Seine is now a party to the internal politics of the Frankish kingdom, and he uses the instrument everybody else uses: somebody's son. It is the last time the record shows him alive.
suggested_refs: Flodoard of Reims, Annals, s.a. 928, the last contemporary notice of Rollo

segments.name: The Handing Over and the Two Deaths

stops.name: Rouen, the land given to Poppa's son
stops.date_confidence: Dudo ch. 13; his chronology here is elastic and fixes no year. Flodoard shows William already acting publicly for his father at Eu in 927 but records no abdication. The transfer is bracketed by William's recognition as ruling prince by 933, when King Raoul granted him Avranches, the Cotentin, and the Channel Islands, lands outside effective Carolingian power. Gerloc's marriage around 936 is attested by van Houts, though Adémar of Chabannes gives her husband as Ebles Manzer instead of his son. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Worn down by age and by war, unable any longer to sit a horse, he calls his men together and hands everything to William, Poppa's son, and takes their oaths to the boy while he is still alive to watch them given. That is the act that turns a war band into a dynasty. Not the grant, not the font: a living man giving away what he holds, and being obeyed. He lives about a year afterward. Gerloc his daughter will be married into Poitou and baptized Adela.
suggested_refs: King Raoul's 933 grant to William Longsword of Avranches, the Cotentin, and the Channel Islands
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 13

stops.name: Rouen, the captives beheaded, as Adémar tells it
stops.date_confidence: Adémar of Chabannes, Chronicon, eleventh century, roughly a century after Rollo; fr.wikipedia dates the alleged sacrifices to 932-933 and calls the anecdote 'douteuse'. It contradicts Dudo's pious deathbed directly and the contradiction is left standing here, not resolved. The figure of 100 captives given in later retellings could not be verified: the De Gruyter/Brill chapter cited for it returns HTTP 403 or 405 on every route, so the number is omitted. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Adémar of Chabannes, writing in the Limousin a century later, has another ending for him. The old man goes out of his mind near death, has Christian prisoners brought out and beheaded before the idols for the gods he was washed clean of, and in the same days sends gold to the churches of Rouen. Both halves in one sentence. Modern historians do not simply throw it out. A people two decades into a coerced baptism, whose priests were being killed in 914, produced this report about its own founder.
suggested_refs: Adémar of Chabannes, Chronicon, the deathbed-sacrifice tradition, against Dudo's pious death
sources: Adémar of Chabannes, Chronicon, reported in fr.wikipedia, 'Rollon'

stops.name: Rouen, migrating full of days
stops.date_confidence: No contemporary source records Rollo's death, its date, or its cause. The bracket runs from 928, Flodoard's last mention of him alive, to 933, Raoul's grant to William; ORB reconstructs it so and 932/933 is the usual figure. English Wikipedia gives 933 outright, following the tomb epitaph, and the pool misreported it as giving a 928-933 bracket. Dudo's 'one year' after the transfer fixes nothing. Month and day default to January.
stops.campa: The other ending is Dudo's, and Dudo's is the one Normandy kept. A year after handing over the land he dies in his bed, too weak to ride, the country quiet behind him, and goes to Christ full of days. He has been in Francia something over forty years, has ruled a piece of it for twenty, and has outlived by four the king who gave it to him. No annal records his death. The kingdom finds out he is gone the way it found out he was there, from what his son does next.
stops.quote: living after that for one year, unable to ride a horse due to his failing age and exhausted body yet keeping the realm pacified, safe and calm... he migrated full of days to Christ
stops.quote_source: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition, ch. 13
suggested_refs: The 928 to 933 bracket on Rollo's death, reconstructed at ORB from Flodoard's sequence
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB ch. 13

segments.name: The Tomb, the Bones, the Bronze

stops.name: Rouen Cathedral, the first layman in the ground
stops.date_confidence: Burial in Rouen Cathedral is tradition, not record, and the claim that he was the first layman buried there is medieval Norman memory. The epitaph exists and its wording is recoverable through fr.wikipedia, 'Rollon', but it is late and commemorative, not a contemporary death record, and it is the source of the flat 933 that later encyclopedias repeat. The cathedral standing today is later than Rollo and the tomb's original position was adjusted afterward. Month arbitrary.
stops.campa: They bury him inside the church he was baptized in, and Norman memory keeps the detail that he is the first layman ever laid in it. A Latin epitaph cut long afterward calls him father and first duke of the Normandy he had himself laid waste, says he was broken by labour, and gives him past eighty in the year 933. Both halves of him are in the inscription, the man who wrecked the country and the man who founded it, in one line and in the same tense.
stops.quote_source: The Latin epitaph at Rollo's tomb, Rouen Cathedral, as given in fr.wikipedia, 'Rollon'
suggested_refs: The ambulatory of Rouen Cathedral, which also holds the heart-tomb of Richard the Lionheart
sources: Presses universitaires de Rouen et du Havre, architectural history of Rouen Cathedral, https://books.openedition.org/purh/3805

stops.name: Rouen, the ducal court commissions the life
stops.date_confidence: Dudo's Historia Normannorum, also called De moribus et actis primorum Normanniae ducum, is dated c. 996-1015 and was written under the patronage of the Norman ducal court; it is court literature, not eyewitness record. Jules Lair established the standard edition in 1865; Felice Lifshitz's English translation follows one eleventh-century manuscript, Berlin Staatsbibliothek Philipps 1854, copied at Mont-Saint-Michel, rather than reconstructing a critical original. The year 1005 is a midpoint of the composition window, not a date of any event.
stops.campa: Three generations after him, Richard II's court sets a canon of Saint-Quentin to write down the family's beginning, and Dudo writes it: the dream of the birds, the Danish inheritance, the ford on the Epte, the foot, the ring in the forest, the pious death. Nearly everything anyone will ever say about Rollo is composed here, at his own seat, by a man who never saw him, for grandsons who need an ancestor who was granted a country rather than one who simply took it.
suggested_refs: Berlin Staatsbibliothek-Preussischer Kulturbesitz, Philipps ms. 1854, copied at Mont-Saint-Michel, the manuscript underlying the Lifshitz translation
sources: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, History of the Normans, trans. Lifshitz, ORB online edition
Jules Lair, ed., Mémoires de la Société des Antiquaires de Normandie (1865)

stops.name: Rouen Cathedral, Maurille moves the bones
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Presses universitaires de Rouen et du Havre architectural history of the cathedral: Archbishop Maurille had the remains transferred in 1063 to a spot near the south door of the Romanesque cathedral then standing. Month not given. The descent from Rollo through William Longsword, Richard I, Richard II, and Robert the Magnificent to William the Conqueror is the standard ducal genealogy, attested piecemeal rather than by any single document.
stops.campa: The bones move because the building is being rebuilt around them, which is the ordinary fate of a founder buried early enough. Archbishop Maurille has the remains taken up and set down again near the south door of the Romanesque cathedral then standing. Three years afterward his great-great-great-grandson William the Conqueror sails for England. From that autumn on, the monument in this church is worth more to Rouen with every year that passes over it.
suggested_refs: Louis Rochet's 1851 equestrian bronze at Falaise, whose plinth names the six dukes before William beginning with Rollo the Norseman
sources: Presses universitaires de Rouen et du Havre, https://books.openedition.org/purh/3805

stops.name: Paris, the parchment in the Marais
stops.date_confidence: The original diploma of 14 March 918 survives as Archives nationales K 16, no. 9. The Paris site, the Hôtel de Soubise and Hôtel de Rohan in the Marais, has held the archives since 1808, and the Paris and Pierrefitte split keeps pre-1790 records in the Marais. Correction to the research pool: its coordinates of 48.8606, 2.3376 fall on the Louvre and Palais-Royal, about 1.6 km west. The 1808 date marks the archives' occupation of the building, not any event in Rollo's life, and the pin is the Soubise rather than the canonical Paris point.
stops.campa: The one contemporary sheet that carries his name comes to rest in the Hôtel de Soubise, where the Archives nationales have kept the records of France before the Revolution since 1808. It is catalogued K 16, number 9. Everything else in this life is a story somebody told afterward, some of it three generations later and some of it eleven centuries later. This is a few lines of chancery Latin with his name in the middle of a clause about an abbey, and it is the whole of the proof.
suggested_refs: Archives nationales, Hôtel de Soubise, Paris, holding K 16 no. 9

stops.name: Rouen, Letellier's Rollo in the town hall garden
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Arsène Letellier's statue of Rollo, in Chauvigny stone, dates from 1865, stands in the garden of the Hôtel de Ville of Rouen, was moved to its present position within that garden in 1956, and has been vandalized repeatedly, a finger amputated and the sword broken. This corrects the widespread claim, carried in the research pool, that the Rouen statue belongs to the 1911 millennium: 1865 is the original and 1911 produced the bronze replicas. Coordinates approximate central Rouen; the exact square was not separately confirmed.
stops.campa: Arsène Letellier cuts him in Chauvigny stone and Rouen sets him up in the garden of the Hôtel de Ville: a bearded Northman, standing, armed, and entirely invented, since no one living or dead ever described his face. What the plinth carries is a nineteenth-century idea of what a Viking chief looked like, worked in soft stone from the Vienne. In 1956 he is moved to another spot in the same garden. He is also attacked more than once over the years. A finger is amputated. The sword is broken off.
suggested_refs: Arsène Letellier's Rollo of 1865, garden of the Hôtel de Ville, Rouen, the original from which the 1911 bronzes were cast

stops.name: Ålesund, the bronze sent north
stops.date_confidence: Attested: two bronze replicas of Letellier's 1865 statue were cast by Alphonse Guilloux for Normandy's millennial celebrations of 1911, one installed at Ålesund. The gift commemorates the Norwegian saga tradition of Gange-Rolv of Giske and is evidence of commemoration, not of birthplace; the Fjord Norway source itself says so. Coordinates mark the town centre; the statue's exact position within Byparken is not separately confirmed. Month and day default to January.
stops.campa: For the thousandth year of Normandy, Rouen has Alphonse Guilloux cast Letellier's Rollo in bronze and sends one of the castings to Ålesund, at the mouth of the fjord country the sagas say he came out of. The gift is Rouen agreeing with Snorri, and it settles nothing: Norway had claimed him for six hundred years already, and Denmark still had Dudo. What arrives is two and a half metres of metal taken off a stone figure carved in Normandy, and it is set up in the town park facing the water.
suggested_refs: Jean-Pierre Chaline, 'Les fêtes du Millénaire de la Normandie: Rouen 1911', Études Normandes 38-3 (1989), 49-68
sources: Fjord Norway, 'The Town Park in Ålesund'

stops.name: Fargo, the third cast
stops.date_confidence: Attested as one of the two 1911 Guilloux bronzes, which pins down the vaguer '20th century' dating carried in the research pool. Not confirmed: the local installation ceremony, the American donor, and the exact site in Fargo, since no Fargo-side source was reached in this pass. Coordinates approximate the city centre; month arbitrary.
stops.campa: The second bronze crosses the Atlantic to Fargo, on the Red River of the North, among Norwegian farmers who came out of those same fjords in the 1870s and the 1880s and named their new townships after the old ones. The Viking founder of a French duchy stands on the North Dakota prairie because the people there are from Møre, and because a French city in 1911 was willing to say so in metal. Who paid for the site, who unveiled it, and where it first stood are not recorded on this side of the water.
suggested_refs: The three Rollo statues: Letellier's 1865 stone at Rouen, and Guilloux's 1911 bronzes at Ålesund and Fargo
sources: Fjord Norway, 'The Town Park in Ålesund'

stops.name: Rouen Cathedral, the effigy burned and the ashes reset
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Presses universitaires de Rouen et du Havre architectural history: before the war the tomb stood in the chapel of the Petit Saint-Romain, last chapel of the south aisle; the effigy there was medieval, resembling and contemporary with William Longsword's gisant, with head and legs remade in the seventeenth century; it was totally destroyed by the wartime bombing; the figure shown today is an actual nineteenth-century copy of Henry the Young King's gisant, not a modern imitation; and after the 1956 restoration what little remained of the ashes was placed under a modern base in the south part of the ambulatory. Month set to the 1944 bombardments of Rouen.
stops.campa: The tomb stands in the chapel of the Petit Saint-Romain, last chapel of the south aisle, and the recumbent figure on it is medieval, of an age with William Longsword's, its head and legs remade in the seventeenth century. In 1944 the bombing of Rouen destroys it outright. What is laid there afterward is a nineteenth-century copy of somebody else's effigy, Henry the Young King's. After the 1956 restoration what little is left of the ashes goes under a modern base in the south ambulatory.
suggested_refs: The chapel of the Petit Saint-Romain, Rouen Cathedral, and the reused nineteenth-century gisant of Henry the Young King
sources: Presses universitaires de Rouen et du Havre, architectural history of Rouen Cathedral, https://books.openedition.org/purh/3805

stops.name: Fécamp, the tombs opened for a chromosome
stops.date_confidence: Attested through Wikipedia's 'Rollo' and 'Fécamp Abbey' articles: the 2016 investigation sampled remains attributed to Richard I and Richard II, one tomb yielding a lower jaw with eight teeth, and radiocarbon showed both sets significantly predated the dukes, one from the third century BCE and one from the eighth century CE. The result is negative evidence about who lies in the Fécamp tombs, not evidence for either origin. The day-precise date comes from the dossier; the underlying press coverage was not re-verified in this pass.
stops.campa: At Fécamp a Norwegian and French team opens the tombs held to be his grandson Richard the Fearless and his great-grandson Richard the Good, meaning to draw a Y chromosome out of the line and find out at last whether the founder was a Dane or a Norwegian. One tomb yields a lower jaw with eight teeth in it. Then the radiocarbon comes back, and neither skeleton is a Norman duke at all: one is from the third century before Christ, the other from the eighth century after.
suggested_refs: The ducal tombs at Fécamp Abbey, opened in 2016 and dated away from the dynasty entirely
